title: Climate policy and climate shocks are being linked to social-protection design, insurance coverage, livelihood security, and the conditions of a just transition
source_unit: International Labour Organization and Agence Française de Développement, Social Protection and Climate Change: The Role of Social Insurance
geography: Global social-protection systems, workers, households, and states facing climate impacts and low-emissions transitions

coverage_gap.value: more than half of the world’s population, including the most vulnerable, still lack basic social-protection coverage

life_cycle_function.value: social protection is framed as coverage against life-cycle risks

climate_threat.value: climate change threatens development gains, poverty reduction, livelihoods, health, living standards, and social equality

observations.method: ILO-AFD report based on a literature review, analytical work, and ILO normative frameworks; the publication states that the underlying analysis was conducted in 2022 and not updated for subsequent developments.
observations.uncertainty: The global coverage statement and analytical findings reflect the report’s original research timeframe; they are not a current administrative census or a causal estimate of climate effects on particular households.
observations.subgroup: Workers, households, informal workers, vulnerable populations, people facing climate hazards, and communities with limited access to social insurance or social assistance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Social protection can buffer climate and life-cycle risk, but eligibility, contribution requirements, benefit adequacy, administrative access, and fiscal capacity can leave exposed groups outside effective protection.

observations.period: 2026 publication; social protection and climate action synergy

denominator.unit: ILO-AFD climate and social-protection linkage frame

shared_goal.value: universal social protection and climate action share the urgent goal of protecting people and planet

adaptation_route.value: social-protection mechanisms can help address the social consequences of climate change and climate policies

policy_integration.value: climate policies should be considered alongside social-protection mechanisms rather than treated as separate domains

observations.method: Conceptual and analytical synthesis of social-protection mechanisms in relation to climate impacts and climate-policy responses.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies a policy synergy but does not provide a standardized implementation model, comparative outcome estimates, or proof that integration produces equitable adaptation.
observations.subgroup: Workers and households exposed to climate shocks, people affected by mitigation policies, governments, social-insurance institutions, employers, and climate-policy implementers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Linking climate and social policy can improve protection, but it can also add administrative complexity, shift costs to contributors, or prioritize transition compensation over deeper changes in exposure and power.

observations.period: 2026 publication; contributory social insurance and just transition

underexamined_route.value: contributory social protection in the context of climate policies has received relatively little attention in existing literature

transition_scope.value: the report connects climate policy, economic and labor-market change, social protection, and the protection of livelihoods and living standards

crisis_learning.value: economic, financial, humanitarian, and COVID-19 crises are used as sources of knowledge about possible climate-related disruption

observations.method: Literature review and analytical work focused on contributory social insurance, informed by ILO normative frameworks and lessons from other crises.
observations.uncertainty: The report’s evidence base is historical and analytical rather than a current evaluation of contributory schemes; crisis analogies may not reproduce climate-risk conditions or distributional effects.
observations.subgroup: Formal and informal workers, employers, contributors, people transitioning between sectors, households facing job or livelihood loss, and social-insurance administrators.
observations.counterinterpretation: Contributory insurance can stabilize transitions for covered workers, while contribution-based systems may exclude informal, precarious, unpaid, migrant, or low-income workers unless subsidies and complementary protection are built in.

analysis_year.unit: year in which the literature review and analytical work were conducted

update_status.value: analysis, data, and references were not updated to incorporate subsequent developments

observations.method: Direct reproduction of the report’s stated evidence-timing and publication-status caveat.
observations.uncertainty: Changes in climate policy, coverage, labor markets, prices, hazards, and social-protection practice after 2022 are outside the underlying analysis.
observations.subgroup: Researchers, policymakers, social-protection institutions, workers, employers, and analysts interpreting the report for current policy decisions.
observations.counterinterpretation: The older evidence base can still provide a useful conceptual foundation, but current decisions require newer data and context-specific evaluation.

related_sources.claim: ILO social-protection and just-transition thematic context, including coverage gaps and climate-vulnerable populations.
Official DOI record for the ILO-AFD publication.

boundary: This record adds a climate-social-protection and just-transition signal linking climate shocks and policies to lifecycle risk, work, household security, social insurance, coverage gaps, and institutional capacity. It is an ILO-AFD literature review and analytical report whose underlying work was conducted in 2022 and not updated, not a current coverage census, household panel, causal evaluation, or proof that contributory social insurance protects excluded workers.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ILO publication page and downloadable report were reviewed for the social-protection coverage gap, climate-risk framing, social-protection/climate-action synergy, contributory-insurance focus, crisis-learning route, and explicit 2022 evidence-timing limitation.
